analogy.p: Imagine a stage shaped like a circle with a spotlight pointing at one section of the edge, the arc. A camera at the exact centre of the stage sees that arc as a wide angle, say 140 degrees. If you move the camera to any seat on the edge of the stage on the far side, the same arc looks narrower: exactly half as wide, 70 degrees. Every seat on that same side sees the same 70 degrees, which is the same segment theorem. A camera at a seat directly opposite the spotlight chord, with the chord being the diameter, always sees a right angle. The analogy breaks down because a real camera has a field of view, while angles in circle theorems are exact geometric angles, and it does not explain the tangent or chord-bisecting results.
analogy.t: The camera at the edge of the stage

bullets: The eight results to know: angle at the centre, angle in a semicircle, angles in the same segment, cyclic quadrilateral, tangent and radius, two tangents from a point, alternate segment, and perpendicular from the centre to a chord.
Questions are typically worth 3 to 5 marks, and 'give reasons for your answer' means every angle statement needs a theorem or rule beside it.
You must be able to **prove** at least the main theorems (angle at the centre, cyclic quadrilateral and alternate segment are the usual ones) using isosceles triangles and angle facts.

Circle theorems are often mixed with other angle facts: angles in a triangle sum to 180 degrees, angles on a straight line sum to 180 degrees, angles round a point sum to 360 degrees, and base angles of an isosceles triangle are equal.
This topic appears on all three papers (Paper 1 non-calculator, Papers 2 and 3 calculator) and is in the Geometry and measures strand, usually near the end of the paper.
Radius, chord and Pythagoras links (right-angled triangle inside a circle) also appear, so some questions mix circle theorems with calculation.
core.h: What the specification asks you to do
core.p: Edexcel GCSE Maths (1MA1) Higher expects you to apply and prove the standard circle theorems concerning **angles, radii, tangents and chords**, and then use them to prove related results. In practice this means two skills. First, you must be able to spot which theorem fits a diagram and use it to calculate a missing angle. Second, you must be able to write a reason for every step in the language of the theorem, because the mark scheme gives a method mark for the calculation and a separate mark for the reason. Proof questions ask 'show that' or 'prove that', and these need a chain of logical statements with a reason for each one.

bullets: **Subtend**: an arc or chord subtends an angle at a point when lines from the point to the ends of the arc or chord form that angle (for example arc AB subtends angle AOB at the centre).

**Segment**: the area cut off by a chord; the bigger one is the major segment and the smaller one is the minor segment. 'Angles in the same segment' means angles at points on the same arc side of the chord.
**Alternate segment**: the segment on the opposite side of the chord from the angle being considered (used in the alternate segment theorem).
**Cyclic quadrilateral**: a four-sided shape with all four vertices on the circumference of a circle.
**Point of contact**: the single point where a tangent touches the circle.
Two radii and a chord always make an **isosceles triangle** (the two radii are equal), which is the key to nearly every proof.
Always draw in extra radii on a diagram; they create isosceles triangles and right angles that unlock the problem.
core.h: Vocabulary of the circle: the words the mark scheme uses
core.p: Before any theorem makes sense you need the exact names of the parts of a circle, because mark schemes use them without explanation. The **centre** is the fixed point that is the same distance from every point on the **circumference**. The **radius** joins the centre to the circumference, and every radius of one circle has the same length. A **chord** is a straight line joining two points on the circumference; the longest chord is the **diameter**, which passes through the centre and is twice the radius. A **tangent** is a straight line that touches the circle at exactly one point and does not cut into it. An **arc** is part of the circumference, and a **segment** is the region between a chord and an arc.

bullets: Write the reason as: 'the angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference'.
Example: angle AOB = 140 degrees, so angle APB = 140 / 2 = 70 degrees. Going the other way, angle APB = 70 degrees means angle AOB = 140 degrees.
Both angles must be subtended by the **same arc or chord**. Check that the arrow from the arc leads to both angles.

The angle at the circumference must be at a point on the **major arc** if the centre angle is the ordinary angle AOB. For a point on the minor arc, the centre angle is the **reflex** angle AOB (more than 180 degrees).
Example with reflex: if angle ACB = 112 degrees with C on the minor arc, the reflex angle AOB = 2 x 112 = 224 degrees, and the ordinary angle AOB = 360 - 224 = 136 degrees.
If the centre O lies on the chord AB (a diameter), the centre angle is 180 degrees, so the angle at the circumference is 90 degrees: this gives the semicircle theorem.
The theorem holds wherever the point P is on the remaining circumference, so the angle APB is the same for every such point P (which is the same-segment theorem).
core.h: Theorem 1: the angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference
core.p: The angle subtended by an arc (or chord) at the centre of a circle is **twice the angle subtended at any point on the remaining part of the circumference**. Both angles must stand on the same arc. For example if the arc AB subtends angle AOB at the centre O and angle APB at a point P on the major arc, then AOB = 2 x APB. This works because the centre angle uses a 'wider' view of the arc: moving the viewing point from the circumference to the centre doubles the angle. It is the master theorem: the semicircle, same segment and cyclic quadrilateral results are all consequences of it.

bullets: Step 1: join PO (and extend to Q); state 'OA = OP (radii)', so triangle OAP is isosceles.
Step 2: base angles of an isosceles triangle are equal, so angle OAP = angle OPA = a.
Step 3: exterior angle of a triangle = sum of the two opposite interior angles, so angle AOQ = 2a.
Step 4: repeat for triangle OBP with base angle b, giving angle BOQ = 2b.
Step 5: angle AOB = 2a + 2b = 2(a + b), and angle APB = a + b, so the angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference.
Alternative reasoning for the exterior angle: angle AOP = 180 - 2a (angles in a triangle), and angle AOQ = 180 - angle AOP (angles on a straight line) = 2a.
Other positions of P (for example when O is outside angle APB) are done by subtracting angles instead of adding; the same two isosceles triangles are used.
In a proof every line needs a reason: radii equal, base angles of an isosceles triangle, exterior angle of a triangle, angles on a straight line.
core.h: Proof of Theorem 1 (angle at the centre)
core.p: You can be asked to prove the angle at the centre theorem, so learn the logic rather than memorising words. Take an arc AB with centre O and a point P on the circumference, and join PO and extend it to a point Q on the other side. Because OA and OP are both radii, triangle OAP is **isosceles**, so angle OAP = angle OPA, which we call a. The angle AOQ is an **exterior angle** of triangle OAP, and an exterior angle equals the sum of the two opposite interior angles, so angle AOQ = a + a = 2a. In the same way triangle OBP is isosceles with base angles b, so angle BOQ = 2b. Adding the two gives angle AOB = 2a + 2b = 2(a + b) = 2 x angle APB.

bullets: Write the reason as: 'the angle in a semicircle is 90 degrees' (or 'angle subtended by a diameter at the circumference is 90 degrees').
Look for a side of a triangle that passes through the centre or is marked as a diameter; that is the signal to use this theorem.

Proof: let O be the centre. OA = OB = OC (radii) so triangles OAC and OBC are isosceles; the base angles are x and y, so the angle at C is x + y, and the angles of triangle ABC give x + y + x + y = 180, so x + y = 90.
Example: AB is a diameter and angle CAB = 34 degrees. Then angle ACB = 90 degrees and angle ABC = 180 - 90 - 34 = 56 degrees.
Pythagoras link: if AB is a diameter of length 10 and AC = 6, then BC = square root of (100 - 36) = 8, because triangle ABC is right-angled at C.
Trigonometry link: in a circle of diameter d, a chord AC that makes angle theta with the diameter AB has length AC = d cos theta.
The converse is used to prove that a line is a diameter or that the centre of a circle lies on a particular side of a triangle.
core.h: Theorem 2: the angle in a semicircle is a right angle
core.p: If AB is a **diameter** of a circle and C is any other point on the circumference, then angle ACB = **90 degrees**. The reason is the angle at the centre theorem: the diameter AB passes through the centre O, so the angle at the centre on the arc AB is the straight angle of 180 degrees, and half of 180 is 90. This result lets you turn a circle problem into a right-angled triangle problem, so you can use Pythagoras' theorem or trigonometry. The converse is also true: if a triangle inscribed in a circle has a right angle, then the side opposite that right angle is a diameter.

bullets: Write the reason as: 'angles in the same segment are equal'.
Example: if angle ACB = 55 degrees, then angle ADB = 55 degrees, and the angle AOB at the centre is 110 degrees.
Both angles must stand on the same chord and lie on the same side of it. Angles on opposite sides of the chord add to 180 degrees instead (cyclic quadrilateral).
When two chords cross inside a circle (for example AC and BD meet at X), triangles ABX and DCX are similar because the angles in the same segment are equal and vertically opposite angles are equal.
Proof: both angles are half of the angle at the centre on the same arc, so they are equal.
A frequent trap: students use this theorem for angles that are on different sides of the chord. Check that C and D are both on the same arc.
Higher tier extension: this theorem is the basis of the 'intersecting chords' result, although the exam only requires you to use the angle result.
core.h: Theorem 3: angles in the same segment are equal
core.p: Angles subtended by the **same arc** (or the same chord) at points on the circumference **in the same segment** are equal. If A and B are two points on a circle and C and D are two other points on the same side of the chord AB, then angle ACB = angle ADB. The reason is that each of them is half of the angle AOB at the centre, so they must equal each other. A useful picture is a butterfly or bow-tie: the chords AD and BC cross inside the circle and you see two equal angles at the two 'wings'. These equal angles are the key to proving that triangles are similar inside a circle.

bullets: Write the reason as: 'opposite angles in a cyclic quadrilateral add up to 180 degrees'.
Example: angle ADC = 112 degrees, so the opposite angle ABC = 180 - 112 = 68 degrees.

An **exterior angle** of a cyclic quadrilateral (extend one side) equals the **interior opposite angle**, because the exterior angle and its adjacent interior angle add to 180 degrees (straight line).
Check that all four vertices lie on the circle; if one does not, the theorem cannot be used.
Converse: if the opposite angles of a quadrilateral add up to 180 degrees, then the quadrilateral is cyclic (useful in proof questions).
A square, rectangle, isosceles trapezium and kite with two right angles are all cyclic quadrilaterals; a general parallelogram or rhombus is not.
Combine with the angle at the centre: if B = 80 degrees then the angle AOC at the centre (on the arc away from B) is 160 degrees.
Common numerical check: the four angles of any quadrilateral sum to 360 degrees, which equals 2 x 180, so a cyclic quadrilateral has two pairs that each sum to 180 degrees.
core.h: Theorem 4: opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral add up to 180 degrees
core.p: A **cyclic quadrilateral** has all four vertices on the circumference, and its **opposite angles sum to 180 degrees**: that is, angle A + angle C = 180 degrees and angle B + angle D = 180 degrees. The reason can be shown with the angle at the centre theorem. If angle B = x, then the arc AC (on the side away from B) subtends 2x at the centre. The opposite vertex D lies on the other arc, which subtends the reflex angle 360 - 2x at the centre, so angle D = (360 - 2x) / 2 = 180 - x. Hence B + D = x + (180 - x) = 180 degrees. This is why quadrilaterals such as a parallelogram (opposite angles equal) can only be cyclic if they are rectangles.

bullets: Write the reason as: 'the angle between a tangent and a radius is 90 degrees' (or 'tangent is perpendicular to the radius').
Always draw in the radius to the point of contact; do this first in every tangent question.
The triangle OTP (O = centre, T = point of contact, P = external point) is right-angled at T, so OP is the hypotenuse.
Example: angle TOP = 40 degrees, then angle OPT = 180 - 90 - 40 = 50 degrees.
A tangent to a circle at the end of a diameter is parallel to the tangent at the other end; both are perpendicular to the diameter.
A line from the centre to the tangent that is perpendicular to the tangent must pass through the point of contact.
Distance from an external point P to the centre O: use OP squared = OT squared + PT squared.
Link to coordinate geometry: the tangent at a point on a circle centred at the origin has gradient equal to the negative reciprocal of the gradient of the radius.
core.h: Theorem 5: a tangent is perpendicular to the radius at the point of contact
core.p: The **tangent** to a circle at a point makes an angle of **90 degrees** with the **radius** drawn to that point of contact. This is because the radius is the shortest distance from the centre to the tangent line, and the shortest distance from a point to a line is the perpendicular. The result gives you a right-angled triangle whenever you see a tangent, so Pythagoras and trigonometry become available. For example, if a tangent from a point P touches a circle of radius 5 cm at T and OP = 13 cm, then PT is the other side of a right-angled triangle: PT = square root of (13 squared - 5 squared) = 12 cm.

bullets: Write the reason as: 'tangents from an external point are equal in length' (or 'the two tangents from a point are equal').
OAPB is a **kite** with right angles at A and B, so angle AOB + angle APB = 180 degrees (sum of the angles in the kite: 90 + 90 + AOB + APB = 360).
Example: angle APB = 50 degrees. Then triangle PAB has base angles (180 - 50) / 2 = 65 degrees, angle OAP = 90, so angle OAB = 90 - 65 = 25 degrees.
Check using the kite: angle AOB = 180 - 50 = 130 degrees, and triangle OAB is isosceles, so angle OAB = (180 - 130) / 2 = 25 degrees (same answer).
Length question: if the radius is 6 cm and OP = 10 cm, each tangent PA = square root of (100 - 36) = 8 cm.
Proof of equal tangents needs the **RHS congruence** condition (right angle, hypotenuse, side): the hypotenuse OP is common, and OA = OB.
The line OP bisects the angle APB, so angle APO = half of angle APB.
In a diagram with two tangents, the first moves are to join O to A and B, and to name the isosceles triangle PAB.
core.h: Theorem 6: tangents from an external point are equal in length
core.p: If two tangents are drawn to a circle from the same external point P, touching the circle at A and B, then **PA = PB** and the triangle PAB is isosceles. The reason is that triangles OAP and OBP are **congruent**: they share the side OP, OA = OB (radii) and both have a right angle at the point of contact (RHS: right angle, hypotenuse, side). Corresponding sides are therefore equal, so PA = PB. The line OP also bisects the angle APB and the angle AOB, which means the figure OAPB is a symmetrical kite with two right angles.

bullets: Write the reason as: 'angle between a tangent and a chord is equal to the angle in the alternate segment'. Using the shorter name 'alternate segment theorem' is also accepted.
To find the equal angle: stand on the chord, look at the angle between the chord and the tangent, then go to the **other side** of the chord to find the angle that subtends the same chord.

Proof: let the tangent-chord angle be x. The radius OT is perpendicular to the tangent so angle OTA = 90 - x. Triangle OTA is isosceles (OT = OA), so angle OAT = 90 - x and angle TOA = 180 - 2(90 - x) = 2x. The angle at the circumference on the alternate segment is half of 2x, which is x.
Example: angle between tangent and chord TA = 48 degrees, so angle TBA in the alternate segment = 48 degrees.
In many problems both angles at the tangent point are used with the triangle angle sum (angles on a straight line add to 180 degrees).
The theorem can be used twice, once on each side of the chord, to find all three angles of a triangle inscribed in a circle with a tangent drawn at one vertex.
Common labelling clue: a tangent line is shown touching the circle at a vertex of a triangle drawn inside the circle.
core.p: The angle between a **tangent** and a **chord** at the point of contact is equal to the angle in the **alternate segment**. The alternate segment is the segment on the opposite side of the chord from the angle you started with. In a diagram with tangent PQ touching the circle at T and chord TA, the angle between the tangent and the chord TA equals the angle TCA at any point C on the arc that lies on the other side of the chord. It is the hardest of the standard theorems to spot, so train yourself to see a tangent and a chord that meet at the same point.

bullets: Write the reason as: 'the perpendicular from the centre to a chord bisects the chord'.
The right-angled triangle has hypotenuse = radius r, one side = distance d from the centre to the chord, and the other side = half the chord length h, so r squared = d squared + h squared.
Example: radius 10 cm, chord 16 cm, so half chord = 8 cm and the distance from the centre d = square root of (100 - 64) = 6 cm.
Reverse example: radius 13 cm, centre is 5 cm from the chord, so half chord = square root of (169 - 25) = 12 cm and the chord = 24 cm.
Equal chords are the same distance from the centre, and a chord closer to the centre is longer.
The perpendicular bisector of any chord passes through the centre of the circle. This fact is used to find the centre of a circle by drawing two chords and their perpendicular bisectors.
Trigonometry link: the angle at the centre is split in half by the perpendicular, so sin (half angle) = half chord / radius.
core.h: Theorem 8: the perpendicular from the centre to a chord bisects the chord
core.p: A line drawn from the centre of a circle perpendicular to a chord **bisects** the chord (it cuts it into two equal halves). Equivalently, the line from the centre to the midpoint of a chord is perpendicular to the chord. The reason is that the two radii to the ends of the chord make an isosceles triangle, and the perpendicular from the apex of an isosceles triangle to its base bisects the base (the two small triangles are congruent by RHS). This is the main route to calculating chord lengths and distances, because the right-angled triangle formed contains the radius as hypotenuse.

bullets: Write each line as 'Angle ABC = 68 degrees because opposite angles in a cyclic quadrilateral add to 180 degrees'. Every statement needs a numerical result and a reason.

Use the basic angle facts alongside the circle theorems: angles in a triangle sum to 180, angles on a straight line sum to 180, angles round a point sum to 360, vertically opposite angles are equal, base angles of an isosceles triangle are equal.
If you cannot see the route, find any angle you can, even if it is not the one asked for; a new angle often unlocks the next step.
Do not measure the diagram: diagrams are 'not accurately drawn', so rely on theorems and calculation only.
Check each answer against the picture for sense (an obtuse angle should be more than 90 degrees).
For 'prove that' questions, state what you are given, define letters for unknown angles (for example let angle OAP = x), and finish with a statement that matches what was asked.
Reasons must be in words: 'angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference' scores, but 'the circle rule' does not.
Wherever you have a tangent, write 'radius is perpendicular to the tangent' and wherever you have a diameter write 'angle in a semicircle'.
core.h: Putting the theorems together: a method for any circle-theorem question
core.p: Real exam questions rarely test one theorem alone; they need a chain of two or three steps and a reason for each. A reliable method is to treat the diagram as a detective problem. First, mark all the information from the question on the diagram, including any given angles, tangents and right angles. Second, draw in extra radii from the centre to any point where a chord or tangent meets the circle, because these create isosceles triangles and right angles. Third, look for the standard patterns (diameter, tangent, cyclic quadrilateral, angles on the same arc) and write angles on the diagram as you find them. Finally, write the answer with each angle statement followed by its reason in brackets.

bullets: **Algebra**: angles given as expressions. For example, in a cyclic quadrilateral angle B = 3x + 10 and angle D = 5x - 30, so 8x - 20 = 180, giving x = 25 and B = 85 degrees.
**Trigonometry**: right angle in a semicircle or tangent-radius triangle lets you use SOHCAHTOA to find lengths.
**Pythagoras**: chord length, tangent length and radius calculations all use right-angled triangles.
**Congruence**: the proof that two tangents are equal uses RHS congruence; the proof that a perpendicular bisects a chord uses congruent triangles.
**Similar triangles**: intersecting chords give similar triangles because angles in the same segment are equal.

**Coordinate geometry**: the equation of a circle with centre the origin is x squared + y squared = r squared, and the tangent at a point is perpendicular to the radius, so its gradient is the negative reciprocal of the radius gradient.
**Sector, arc and segment work**: the angle at the centre links to arc length and area of sectors.
**Proof**: expect to write formal proof lines with reasons; practise a short list of the standard proofs until you can write them from memory.
core.h: Link to other topics and Higher tier extension
core.p: Circle theorems connect strongly to other parts of GCSE geometry. They use isosceles triangle facts, congruence (RHS), similar triangles, Pythagoras' theorem, trigonometry and proof. Understanding these links makes the theorems feel like logical consequences rather than facts to memorise. At Higher tier, circle theorems are also combined with algebra: angles are given as expressions like 2x + 10 and (3x - 20), and you must form and solve an equation. Questions also mix circle theorems with vectors, equations of circles and the equation of a tangent in coordinate geometry.

exam: Command words: 'Work out' and 'Find' need a numerical answer with working; 'Give reasons for your answer' means a theorem name beside each angle; 'Prove' or 'Show that' needs a complete logical chain ending in the statement given.
Mark allocation: a simple one-theorem angle with reason is 2 marks (1 for the angle, 1 for the reason). A two-step question is 3 or 4 marks. A 'prove' question is usually 3 to 5 marks.

Reasons the mark scheme accepts: 'angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference', 'angle in a semicircle is 90 degrees', 'angles in the same segment are equal', 'opposite angles in a cyclic quadrilateral add up to 180 degrees', 'angle between tangent and radius is 90 degrees', 'tangents from an external point are equal', 'alternate segment theorem' (or in full), 'perpendicular from the centre to a chord bisects the chord'.
Always mark the information on the diagram as you go: write each new angle on the picture so you can use it in later steps.
Draw extra radii. A line from the centre to the point where a chord or tangent meets the circle usually creates an isosceles triangle or a right angle.
Use the basic angle facts as steps too (triangle sum 180, straight line 180, isosceles base angles, vertically opposite) and give reasons for them as well.
For algebraic angle questions, form an equation from the theorem (for example 3x + 10 + 5x - 30 = 180) and solve it, then substitute back to find the angles.
For a proof question, define letters for angles (for example let angle OAB = x), argue in order, give a reason on each line, and finish with a conclusion sentence that matches the question.
Chord and tangent length questions: draw the right-angled triangle, state which theorem gives the right angle, then use Pythagoras. Include units for lengths.
Check your final angle against the diagram for sense, and make sure angles that must sum to 180 degrees do so.

mistakes.r: Give the full theorem in words, for example 'angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference'. Vague reasons score no reason marks.
mistakes.w: Writing 'circle theorem' or 'angles in a circle' as the reason.

mistakes.r: Both angles must be subtended by the same arc. Check that the arc leads to the angle at O and to the angle at the circumference.
mistakes.w: Using the angle at the centre theorem when the angle is not at the centre, or applying it to different arcs.

mistakes.r: Angles on opposite sides of the chord are in different segments and add to 180 degrees (cyclic quadrilateral).
mistakes.w: Treating angles in the same segment as equal when they are on opposite sides of the chord.

mistakes.r: Always draw the radius first; it makes a 90 degree angle and an isosceles triangle with another radius.
mistakes.w: Forgetting to draw the radius to the point of contact of a tangent.

mistakes.r: The equal angle is in the segment on the OTHER side of the chord from the tangent angle.
mistakes.w: Using the alternate segment theorem with the wrong angle (the angle in the same segment).

mistakes.r: Diagrams are 'not accurately drawn'; calculate every angle using theorems.
mistakes.w: Measuring angles from the diagram with a protractor.

mistakes.r: Only a quadrilateral with all four vertices on the circle is cyclic. State this before using the opposite-angle rule.
mistakes.w: Thinking any quadrilateral with a circle nearby is cyclic.

mistakes.r: Opposite angles in a cyclic quadrilateral SUM to 180 degrees; they are equal only in a rectangle.
mistakes.w: Saying 'opposite angles are equal' for a cyclic quadrilateral.

mistakes.r: The perpendicular from the centre bisects the chord, so use HALF the chord with the radius as hypotenuse.
mistakes.w: In a chord question, using the whole chord length as one side of the right-angled triangle.

mistakes.r: Write each angle with its reason; the reasons carry their own marks even when the final value is correct.
mistakes.w: Giving the answer with no working or no reasons for a 'give reasons' question.

summary: The specification asks you to **apply and prove the standard circle theorems** about angles, radii, tangents and chords, and to use them to prove related results and to find missing angles with clear reasons. It matters because circle-theorem questions are among the most reliably tested Higher geometry questions: they are usually 3 to 6 marks, and every mark depends on naming the correct theorem in the correct words.

terms.d: An arc or chord subtends an angle at a point when the lines from that point to the ends of the arc or chord form that angle.
A straight line segment joining two points on the circumference of a circle.
A chord that passes through the centre of the circle; it is twice the length of the radius.
A straight line that touches a circle at exactly one point, the point of contact, without crossing into the circle.
A part of the circumference of a circle.
The region of a circle between a chord and an arc; the major segment is the larger and the minor segment the smaller.
The segment on the opposite side of a chord from the angle between the chord and the tangent.
A quadrilateral with all four vertices on the circumference of a circle; opposite angles add up to 180 degrees.
The single point where a tangent touches a circle; the radius to this point is perpendicular to the tangent.
The angle in a semicircle is a right angle: the angle subtended by a diameter at the circumference is 90 degrees.
The angle subtended by an arc at the centre is twice the angle subtended at the circumference by the same arc.
The angle between a tangent and a chord at the point of contact is equal to the angle in the alternate segment.
To cut into two equal parts; the perpendicular from the centre of a circle to a chord bisects the chord.
A triangle with two equal sides and two equal base angles; two radii and a chord always form one.
Two right-angled triangles are congruent if they have equal hypotenuses and one other pair of equal sides.
An angle formed by extending one side of a triangle; it equals the sum of the two opposite interior angles.

worked.ans: (a) Angle ABC = 68 degrees, because opposite angles in a cyclic quadrilateral add up to 180 degrees. (b) Reflex angle AOC = 224 degrees, because the angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference.
worked.q: A, B, C and D are points on a circle with centre O. Angle ADC = 112 degrees. (a) Work out angle ABC. (b) Work out the reflex angle AOC. Give a reason for each answer. (4 marks)
steps: ABCD is a cyclic quadrilateral because all four points lie on the circle.
Angle ABC and angle ADC are opposite angles, so they add up to 180 degrees (M1). Angle ABC = 180 - 112 = 68 degrees (A1).
Angle ADC = 112 degrees is an angle at the circumference on arc AC (the side away from D).
The angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference, so reflex angle AOC = 2 x 112 = 224 degrees (M1, A1).
Check: the other angle AOC = 360 - 224 = 136 degrees = 2 x 68, which agrees with angle ABC = 68 degrees.

worked.ans: Angle OAB = 25 degrees, because PA = PB (tangents from an external point), the angle between tangent and radius is 90 degrees, and angles in a triangle sum to 180 degrees.
worked.q: PA and PB are tangents from P to a circle with centre O. A and B are points on the circle. Angle APB = 50 degrees. Work out angle OAB. Give reasons. (4 marks)
steps: Tangents from an external point are equal, so PA = PB and triangle PAB is isosceles (B1).
Angle PAB = (180 - 50) / 2 = 65 degrees, because the base angles of an isosceles triangle are equal and angles in a triangle sum to 180 degrees (M1).
OA is a radius and PA is a tangent, so angle OAP = 90 degrees (the angle between a tangent and a radius is 90 degrees) (M1).
Angle OAB = angle OAP - angle PAB = 90 - 65 = 25 degrees (A1).
Check: angle AOB = 360 - 90 - 90 - 50 = 130 degrees (kite), and triangle OAB is isosceles, so angle OAB = (180 - 130) / 2 = 25 degrees.

worked.ans: Angle TBA = 48 degrees, angle TAB = 70 degrees, angle ATB = 62 degrees. Reasons: alternate segment theorem (twice) and angles on a straight line add up to 180 degrees.
worked.q: The line PQ is a tangent to the circle at T. A and B are points on the circle. Angle PTA = 48 degrees and angle QTB = 70 degrees. Work out the three angles of triangle ATB, giving a reason for each. (5 marks)
steps: The angle between the tangent PT and the chord TA is 48 degrees. By the alternate segment theorem, angle TBA (in the alternate segment) = 48 degrees (M1, A1).
The angle between the tangent TQ and the chord TB is 70 degrees. By the alternate segment theorem, angle TAB = 70 degrees (M1, A1).
Angles on a straight line PQ add to 180 degrees, so angle ATB = 180 - 48 - 70 = 62 degrees (A1).
Check: 48 + 70 + 62 = 180 degrees, which is the sum of the angles in a triangle.
